opus-5.5.text:
I think there isn't one fixed ratio. It depends a lot on what stage your team is in and what you're betting on. But I can share how I think about it.

First, I'd separate compute that is "producing" from compute that is "exploring." Pretraining and large post-training runs are production. Once you've decided on the recipe, you need to commit a big, stable block of GPUs, because a big run that keeps getting interrupted or squeezed is very wasteful. So that part should be protected.

But I think many teams under-allocate research compute. Some people see small experiments as a cost. In my experience, most of the real gains come from the many small-scale ablations you run before the big run: data mixture, architecture tweaks, training stability, RL recipes. If you don't have enough exploration compute, you end up making big bets based on intuition, and a single failed large run costs far more than all those small experiments combined. So I'd rather give researchers a generous, flexible pool and let them iterate quickly.

Post-training has become much more compute-hungry than before, especially with reinforcement learning. It used to be a small fraction compared with pretraining. Now, with long reasoning chains and large-scale RL, rollouts are expensive, and RL itself is partly inference. So the boundary between inference and training is getting blurry. I think the infrastructure should let you move resources between rollout generation and training dynamically, instead of rigidly splitting them.

Inference for serving users is different again. It's driven by demand, and you can't really cut it if people are using your product. But a lot of efficiency can be squeezed there: better kernels, MoE, quantization, speculative decoding. Every bit you save on serving can go back to research. That's why I care about model efficiency. It's not only about cost to users; it directly decides how much you can explore.

So if I had to summarize: protect the big runs, be generous with research, treat RL as a first-class consumer rather than an afterthought, and keep pushing inference efficiency so it doesn't eat everything. And above all, the allocation should be revisited constantly. The field changes every few months, and a ratio that made sense half a year ago may be completely wrong today.

r001.rationale: The response says serving inference is driven by demand and cannot really be cut when users are using the product.

r002.rationale: It recommends protecting pretraining runs and treating post-training as a first-class compute consumer, but does not recommend comparable investment in the two.

r003.rationale: It calls for generous, flexible research compute but does not say research should receive more GPUs than pretraining and post-training combined.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, this is one of the hardest questions any lab faces, and I don't think there's a clean formula. But let me share how I think about it.

The first thing to say is that these four buckets are not actually independent. People talk about them as if you're dividing a pie, but inference and training feed each other. If your model is serving real users, that traffic tells you where the model fails, and that becomes the most valuable signal for the next round of post-training. If you starve inference to protect pretraining, you lose that loop. So I don't think of inference as a cost center that competes with research. It's part of the research pipeline.

That said, there is a real tension, and it shows up at the margin. Pretraining is the most capital-intensive and the least reversible. Once you commit a big cluster to a run for two or three months, you can't take it back halfway. So the decision to launch a large pretraining run has to be made with much more care than anything else. My view is that you should not be running big pretraining runs continuously. You run them when you have accumulated enough from research: new data recipes, architecture changes, scaling insights, things that have been validated at small scale. The pretraining run is the harvest, not the farming.

Which brings me to research. This is where I would protect compute most aggressively, even when the pressure is to cut it. Research compute is small per experiment, but it needs to be available and fast. The worst thing you can do to a researcher is make them wait a week for a slot, because then they stop trying ideas. A lot of the real advances come from someone running a weird experiment on a few hundred GPUs over a weekend. If you look at how the efficient models in the last couple of years came about, the ideas were mostly validated at modest scale first. So I'd rather have research run on a reserved, somewhat underutilized pool than squeeze it to maximize utilization numbers. Utilization is a misleading metric for research.

Post-training is the bucket that has grown the most, especially with reinforcement learning on reasoning. A few years ago post-training was maybe a few percent of total training compute. Now with RL, with long rollouts, with verifiers, it can approach or even rival pretraining in some setups. And it's much more iterative. You run, you look, you adjust the reward, you run again. So it needs a different kind of scheduling. It needs elasticity rather than one giant fixed block.

If you force me to give rough numbers, I'd say for a lab that is also serving products, something like a quarter to a third goes to inference, but you want that number to grow because it means you have users. Pretraining is bursty, maybe a third on average but zero most of the time and nearly everything during a run. Post-training and research together take the rest, and I'd want research to never drop below ten to fifteen percent no matter how tight things get.

But the real answer is that the allocation should be dynamic and the organization has to be willing to reshuffle quickly. The labs that do well are the ones where a researcher can say, this experiment is working, and get scaled up within days, not quarters. Rigid budgets are how you miss the next thing.

r001.rationale: The response says inference should take roughly a quarter to a third of compute in a product-serving lab and that this share should grow as the lab gains users, linking inference allocation to usage demand.

r002.rationale: It says post-training can approach or rival pretraining in some setups, but this is descriptive; it does not recommend comparable compute investment for the two.

r003.rationale: It protects research compute and sets a 10–15% floor, but does not recommend allocating more GPUs to research than to pretraining and post-training combined.

astra-6.text:
I’d start with the bottleneck rather than a fixed percentage. Inference needs enough capacity to serve users reliably, but we also need to protect compute for research. Otherwise, immediate demand can consume everything, and we lose the ability to improve the next generation of models.

For pretraining and post-training, the balance depends on what we’re trying to improve. If we need stronger underlying capabilities, that argues for pretraining. If the model has the capability but doesn’t use it reliably or follow instructions well, post-training may be the better investment.

I’d reserve a stable pool for exploratory research, guarantee a baseline for inference, and allocate the remaining resources around specific experiments and training milestones. Then I’d revisit that allocation based on results. The key is to ask what each additional unit of compute is actually buying us.

r001.rationale: It says inference needs enough capacity to serve users reliably, but does not state that compute needs vary with scenario-specific usage demand.

r002.rationale: It describes choosing between pretraining and post-training based on the goal, but does not recommend comparable compute investment in them.

r003.rationale: It recommends protecting a stable pool for research, but does not say research should receive more GPUs than pretraining and post-training combined.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think there’s a fixed ratio that works for every team. I would start by protecting enough inference capacity to serve users reliably, and enough research capacity that researchers can test ideas without spending most of their time waiting for GPUs.

Then I’d allocate the remaining compute according to the bottleneck. If the base model is missing fundamental capabilities, pretraining deserves more investment. If those capabilities are already there but the model struggles to use them consistently, post-training may give us more value per GPU-hour.

Research also needs a path from small experiments to larger runs. We should validate an idea at a modest scale, then commit more resources when the evidence supports it. Otherwise, one large training run can crowd out many experiments that might change our direction.

So I’d keep the allocation flexible and revisit it as we learn. The question is: what would the next unit of compute actually help us discover or improve?

r001.rationale: It says to protect enough inference capacity for reliable service, but does not tie that capacity to scenario-specific usage demand.

r002.rationale: It suggests adjusting pretraining and post-training based on the model’s bottleneck, not investing comparably in both.

r003.rationale: It recommends enough research capacity for experiments but does not say research should receive more GPUs than pretraining and post-training combined.
